title: ISP: Interface Segregation Principle
description: Small, role-shaped interfaces: fat interfaces, empty implementations and how to split them without exploding the count.

questions.text: What is the Interface Segregation Principle?

options.text: Interfaces must have a single method
Each class must have its own interface
No client should be forced to depend on methods it does not use
Interfaces should be as large as possible

questions.explanation: Clients should see only the methods they need. A big interface couples every client to changes that do not concern them.

questions.text: A `Machine` interface has `print()`, `scan()` and `fax()`. A basic printer implements it and throws on `scan` and `fax`. What is the fix?

options.text: Make the printer return null for scanning
Delete `fax()`
Keep the interface and document the exceptions
Split it into `Printer`, `Scanner` and `FaxMachine` and let a multi-function device implement all three

questions.explanation: Role interfaces let a simple printer implement only `Printer`. The throwing stubs were a sign that the interface lumped separate roles together.

questions.text: Which smell most reliably points at an ISP violation?

options.text: A method with default arguments
A long class name
A class with a private constructor
An implementing class with several empty or "not supported" methods

questions.explanation: Methods a class cannot honestly implement are the clearest signal that the interface asks for more than some implementers can give.

questions.text: Why does a fat interface hurt the callers?

options.text: It makes the code slower
A change to a method one caller never uses still forces that caller to be recompiled, retested or redeployed
It prevents polymorphism
It requires a base class

questions.explanation: Dependence on unused methods means unrelated changes ripple to you. Narrow interfaces shrink the blast radius of a change.

questions.text: Splitting every interface down to a single method is always the best application of ISP.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: False. Interfaces should follow roles that clients really use together. One method per interface produces a pile of tiny types with no meaning, so group methods that always travel together.

questions.text: A service only needs to read users, yet it depends on a `UserRepository` with save, delete and reindex methods. What does ISP suggest?

options.text: Add a mock for each method
Pass the whole repository and trust the developer
Make the repository static
Define a narrow `UserReader` (or query) interface for that service

questions.explanation: Depend on the slice you use. The same implementation can still satisfy both the wide and the narrow interface.

questions.text: Which are benefits of role-shaped interfaces?

options.text: Fewer unrelated changes ripple into a client
It is easier to see what a client really needs
Tests need smaller fakes
Implementations never need any code

questions.explanation: Small interfaces make fakes tiny, limit ripple effects and document dependencies. They do not remove the work of implementing behaviour.

questions.text: In Go, small interfaces like `io.Reader` are idiomatic. Which principle does that style most directly reflect?

options.text: Interface Segregation
Single Responsibility only
Open/Closed only
Singleton

questions.explanation: `io.Reader` has one method, and a type satisfies it implicitly. Consumers declare the small interface they need, which is ISP taken to its natural conclusion.
